question.text: Priya, aged 35, is a first-time investor who wants to save tax under Section 80C (available under the old tax regime) but is worried about equity market volatility. She has never invested in mutual funds before. Which scheme type would address both her needs?

answer.text: Small-cap fund -- it offers the highest growth potential
Gilt fund -- it is safe as it invests in government securities
ELSS fund via SIP -- it provides tax saving under Section 80C (old tax regime) and SIP reduces the impact of volatility through rupee cost averaging
Credit risk fund -- it offers higher returns than fixed deposits

explanation.text: The Logic: ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme) is the only mutual fund category eligible for deduction under Section 80C, and that deduction is available under the old tax regime. ELSS carries a statutory three-year lock-in, which gives equity time to perform and discourages premature exits. Investing via SIP, as the workbook explains, smooths the entry price across cycles through rupee cost averaging, addressing Priya's volatility concerns. The Trap: Small-cap funds are too volatile for a nervous first-time investor. Gilt funds and credit risk funds do not qualify for Section 80C, regardless of regime. ELSS is the only mutual fund route to the 80C benefit, and that benefit applies under the old tax regime. Note: Always pair the ELSS-80C answer with the old-tax-regime qualifier, and tie the volatility-management story to the SIP rupee-cost-averaging mechanism described in the workbook.
